    22→| Trigger | Path | Decision body | Typical duration |

    33→
    34→Note: ESPA is normally submitted **after** DSD site plan approval, not before (AEDC 1.4.2.7.A). Build the AE design into the diligence timeline as a post-approval, pre-permit critical path item — not as a parallel-with-site-plan item.
    35→
    36→## Constraints to evaluate
    37→
    38→### Overhead clearance & undergrounding
    39→
    40→- **Building footprint vs. 15-ft radial / 7.5-ft sky-to-ground clearance** from any AE overhead distribution conductor on or adjacent to the site (UCM § 1.10.3). Both apply simultaneously; the outer conductor (not pole centerline) is the datum. Evaluate whether the desired building envelope physically clears overhead lines along the relevant frontage, and if not, whether undergrounding the offending span is feasible and at what cost.
    41→- **10-ft overhead utility zone** from energized conductor where overhead lines remain on a Core Transit Corridor or Urban Roadway frontage (LDC Subchapter E § 2.2.2.B.3.b; § 2.2.3.B.3). Same 10-ft zone applies inside Plaza Saltillo TOD (§ 3.3.2.A.3.b) and NBG (§ 3.3.2.B.4.b). Confirm whether the frontage street triggers Subchapter E or a regulating plan, then whether overhead is feasible to underground vs. relocate to rear-of-site.
    42→- **Building-to-property-line undergrounding** mandatory on all CTC, Urban Roadway, Plaza Saltillo TOD, NBG, and Hill Country Roadway Corridor frontages (LDC Subchapter E § 2.2.2.B.3.a, § 2.2.3.B.3; Plaza Saltillo TOD § 3.3.2.A.3 / .3.3.A.3 / .3.4.A.3; NBG § 3.3.2.B.4.a; LDC § 25-2-1125). Budget service-lateral undergrounding cost.
    43→- **ROW undergrounding "to the maximum extent practicable"** on the same frontages (same citations). This is judgment-driven; expect AE to negotiate which existing overhead is left in place vs. relocated to rear of site. Identify the existing overhead pattern early.
    44→- **Transmission proximity** (60 kV+: 69 / 138 / 345 kV AE circuits): clearance envelopes are site-specific and require AE engineering (UCM § 1.14.3.1); circuits cannot be de-energized for nearby work. If a transmission line or labeled transmission easement abuts the site, treat as a binding envelope constraint and engage AE Transmission before locking massing. 25-ft × 16-ft vertical ROW access corridor must be preserved throughout construction (UCM § 1.14.4); plat notes per AEDC 1.16.0(8) become mandatory.
    45→- **Service-drop vertical clearance** over driveways and access — 16 ft (no-truck) / 18 ft (truck/public street) (UCM § 1.10.6.2). Constrains canopy/porte-cochère height and loading-dock geometry.
    46→
    47→### Underground routing & easements
    48→
    49→- **AW planting-zone prohibition** (UCM § 2.9.1.C): no AW main, service, or appurtenance within the ROW street-tree planting zone. Root barriers required 7 ft from trunk; 2-ft AW offset from barrier; minimum 8-ft Street Tree Utility Gap between zones. Constrains where water service can leave the building when street trees are required.
    50→- **No parallel routing within AE / public utility easement** (UCM § 2.9.1.A.3) — only perpendicular or up to 45° crossings. Constrains site utility layout when easements bisect the parcel.
    51→- **Easement encroachment**: no permanent structures, pools, or buildings in AE easements (UCM § 1.10.10.2); landscaping/paving/walls in private AE easements require License Agreement from AE Public Involvement (UCM § 1.10.10.3); same items in public utility easements / public ROW require Chapter 14 license (§ 14-11-41). Evaluate whether the desired site plan crosses easements and whether the licensing pathway is workable.
    52→- **Transformer pad siting** (UCM §§ 1.5.2.6, 1.10.4): hot-stick (padlocked) side 10 ft from any adjacent building; non-operator sides 3 ft from fence; operator side 5 ft; pad within 6 ft of paved truck-accessible surface; pad must be on customer property (not ROW or parkland); dedicated AE easement encumbers the pad. Reserve ~150–250 sf of usable frontage for the pad early in concept design.
    53→- **AE truck access** (UCM § 1.3.16): 12-ft horizontal × 16-ft vertical clear path to AE equipment, with 20 × 35 ft set-up area at 35-ft vertical clearance. AE facilities normally at front of property or adjacent to paved surface (UCM § 1.3.15).
    54→- **AE underground separations** (UCM § 1.10.5.A): 12 in min from other utilities at perpendicular crossings; 36 in from ≥60 psi gas. Joint trench with other utilities requires written AE agreement.
    55→- **Water/wastewater main crossings** (UCM § 2.9.1.B.3, § 2.9.2.B.17): 12 in (AW above) / 18 in (AW below) for open-cut; trenchless = greater of 2× excavation diameter or 36 in.
    56→- **ROW assignment / 24-in proximity** (§ 14-11-180(C)): facilities within 24 in of an existing ROW facility require AULCC ROW assignment change approval — a process, not a prohibition, but it consumes time.
    57→- **Light rail corridors**: UCM § 5.2.2 Downtown Rail Corridor Permit for E-W 4th Street corridor (IH-35 to Seaholm); UROP consultation for other Project Connect alignments. Materially affects feasibility for parcels along Project Connect.
    58→- **Moonlight towers** (downtown / central Austin): 25-ft ROW-installation prohibition (§ 14-11-205); 100-ft permit threshold for any construction near tower or guy wire (§ 14-11-201). Locations are not mapped in code — confirm by field survey early if site is in downtown or central Austin.
    59→
    60→### Drainage-utility interactions
    61→
    62→- **SCM staging area + maintenance access drive vertical clearance**: 14 ft from existing/proposed vegetation at maturity (DCM § 1.2.4.E.2.e and § 1.2.4.E.1.e.ii). Applies to COA-maintained and residential-development SCMs above 5,000 cf / 3-ft depth thresholds. Constrains canopy planting along maintenance routes.
    63→- **No utility routing under detention/retention ponds** (reviewer convention; common-violation pattern). Affects site utility layout when ponds dominate the site.
    64→- **Storm drain manhole vs. AE pole separation**: minimum 5 ft horizontal between storm drain manholes and AE overhead poles (reviewer convention). Constrains drainage outfall layout where existing poles are present.
    65→- **Encasement under roads/structures** (UCM § 2.9.1.D): encased crossings under roadways require material, dimensional, and longitudinal extent specifications on plans. Budget bored/encased crossings on any utility leaving the site under a public street.
    66→
    67→### Construction-phase impacts
    68→
    69→- **Transmission demolition sequence** (UCM § 1.14.9): pre-construction safety meeting ≥48 hr before work; barricades 10 ft from all transmission structures including guys/anchors; warning signs under overhead facilities; no spoils or materials in transmission easement; crane and temporary-structure setbacks so they cannot fall within 20 ft of transmission. Forces an alternate spoils/laydown area when transmission abuts the site.
    70→- **Work-zone vertical clearance below overhead** (UCM § 1.10.6.2; § 1.3.16): 18 ft where truck traffic is anticipated; 16 ft for affirmatively non-truck driveways; 35 ft set-up area in front of AE equipment. Affects crane staging and tilt-up sequencing.
    71→
    72→### Connectivity & frontage
    73→
    74→- **Table B utility-in-drive-aisle option** (LDC Subchapter E § 2.3.1.B.2): on subject sites (≥3 ac nonresidential, or surface parking between building and principal street), site must select ≥2 Table B options (3 if parking >125% of formerly required). Routing utilities under parking stalls is only a deficiency if utility-in-drive-aisle is the selected option but not implemented, or if Table B count is otherwise short. Evaluate whether the site can hit its Table B count without forcing utilities under parking.
    75→
    76→### Administrative & service-capacity
    77→
    78→- **AE Service Availability Letter** (AEDC § 1.4.1) — only where it is unclear which utility serves the site. Confirm AE service area on edge-of-territory parcels before design.
    79→- **Service capacity**: AE Design has sole authority over available voltage / service characteristics (AEDC § 1.3.2). For large loads (>320 A continuous → instrument-rated CT service per AEDC § 1.4.0; or any Network Area service downtown), engage AE Design early; available capacity at the nearest feeder may itself be a constraint.
    80→- **Street lighting**: AE develops the lighting installation plan. Developer responsibilities differ by location (AEDC §§ 1.6.4–1.6.7). Inside the Great Streets boundary (MLK / Lady Bird Lake / IH-35 / Lamar), Chapter 6 dictates fixture type (Gardco Circa/Form 10; Kim ERA), spacing (8 poles/block), and mounting heights (24-ft street / 12-ft pedestrian) — non-standard poles permitted at developer cost differential.
    81→- **Four mandatory Standard AE Plan Notes** (verbatim) plus AEDC § 1.16.0(7) site-specific notes. Missing or altered text = rejection. Low-effort compliance issue but a frequent rejection cause.
    82→- **AULCC Completeness Letter** gates ROW Review approval.
    83→- **Addressing plan approval** (AMS) — distinct from an Address Validation Letter; AVL is **not** an approved addressing plan (common confusion). Gates site plan approval when new addresses or street names are involved.
    84→
    85→## Opportunities to evaluate
    86→
    87→- **Frontage selection on corner lots**: CTC designation takes priority as principal street; if a non-CTC corner is the practical service frontage, undergrounding cost may concentrate there. Conversely, choosing the non-CTC face for the building front can avoid the 10-ft overhead zone constraint on the CTC frontage entirely.
    88→- **CTC short-lot alternative tree exception** (LDC Subchapter E § 2.2.2.B.3.c; Plaza Saltillo TOD § 3.3.2.A.3.c): on lots ≤120 ft deep, utility-compatible alternative tree species may be used **beneath** the overhead utilities rather than offset from them. Avoids removing/relocating street trees to clear an overhead corridor.
    89→- **Plaza Saltillo TOD § 3.3.2.A.3.c facade-setback alternative**: same alternative-tree path also available when full compliance would push the facade ≥30 ft beyond the curb face. Material on tight TOD parcels.
    90→- **AE relocation at customer expense** (UCM § 1.3.19): AE will relocate facilities at the customer's expense where feasible; build the cost into the pro forma rather than treating overhead as immovable. Note that AE will not relocate to an adjacent property without that owner's written consent — that consent is a feasibility variable.
    91→- **UCM § 2.9.6 waiver pathway**: applicants who cannot meet UCM § 2 requirements have a formal waiver route. Worth evaluating on constrained urban sites instead of forcing a redesign.
    92→- **Sub-AULCC-threshold scoping**: if ROW utility work can be kept below 300 LF citywide (or 25 LF in DAPCZ), with no pole relocations and no main assignments, AULCC review is avoided entirely. On small infill projects this can compress the schedule by 2–4 months — evaluate whether trenching can be confined to private property.
    93→- **Rear-of-site undergrounding** vs. front-frontage undergrounding: where alley or rear access exists, "maximum extent practicable" can be argued for relocation to the rear, sometimes reducing the lateral length compared with undergrounding the entire frontage span.
    94→- **Service-Only ESPA path**: keeping the total load under 350 A single-phase / 225 A three-phase (non-network) keeps the project on the Service-Only path and out of Design Services — a meaningful schedule compression where load can be managed.
    95→- **AE License Agreement vs. easement relocation**: many AE-easement encroachments (paving, retaining walls, landscaping) can be resolved through a License Agreement from AE Public Involvement (UCM § 1.10.10.3) rather than relocating the easement. Faster and cheaper, when AE will agree.
    96→- **Plat-note compliance for transmission easements**: where a transmission easement crosses the site, the AEDC § 1.16.0(8) plat notes (AE tree pruning, additional easement provision, erosion control, NESC clearance, 24-hr AE access, 48,000-lb axle load roads, 48-hr notice) are mandatory but can be added to the plat at low cost — treat as administrative, not feasibility-blocking, unless coupled with a physical envelope conflict.

    99→
   100→- **environmental.md** / **GIS** — Plaza Saltillo TOD boundary, NBG boundary, CTC/Urban Roadway frontage classification, Hill Country Roadway Corridor proximity (1,000 ft of named roadways), DAPCZ boundary (Code § 14-11-161(7)), Great Streets boundary, light rail corridor proximity, parkland boundaries.
   101→- **utility-survey.md** — existing overhead and underground AE facilities on or adjacent to site (poles, conductors, vaults, transformers, guys/anchors); transmission easement boundaries; existing AE easements / PUEs; existing ROW utilities (AW mains, gas, telecom); existing moonlight towers if downtown/central.
   102→- **transportation.md** — frontage street classifications; truck-access expectations (for service-drop 16 vs. 18 ft determination); driveway locations.
   103→- **property-records.md** — recorded easements (private AE, PUE, transmission, drainage); plat notes referencing transmission easement obligations.
   104→- **zoning.md** — base zoning + any regulating-plan overlay (Plaza Saltillo TOD subdistrict, NBG subdistrict prefix TOD/CMU/NMU/NR/WMU/CI, UNO, ERC, downtown).
   105→- **program intent** — service-load estimate (amps / phase), continuous-load expectation, presence of vaults or generators, exterior wall modifications (for BSPA trigger).
   106→
   107→## Output structure
   108→
   109→Standard discipline output shape — see `references/phase3-disciplines.md`.

   111→## Severity heuristics
   112→
   113→| Finding | Severity |
   114→|---|---|
   115→| Transmission line on or abutting site with envelope conflict that cannot be cleared without relocating the line | `significant` |
   116→| AE service capacity insufficient at the nearest feeder for projected load (Network Area downtown or large industrial) | `significant` |
   117→| Required overhead-to-underground conversion along entire CTC/Urban Roadway frontage materially impacts pro forma | `significant` |
   118→| Site within 25 ft of a moonlight tower (ROW prohibition) blocking proposed ROW work | `significant` |
   119→| 10-ft overhead utility zone (Subchapter E / Plaza Saltillo / NBG) crosses desired building footprint with no short-lot alternative-tree exception | `significant` |
   120→| AULCC trigger met (≥300 LF citywide, ≥25 LF DAPCZ, pole relocation, main assignment) — adds 2–4 months schedule | `moderate` |
   121→| Hill Country Roadway Corridor — all on-site utilities must go underground; cost adder vs. mixed-mode | `moderate` |
   122→| Transformer pad placement constrains frontage usable width or requires AE easement reservation | `moderate` |
   123→| AW planting-zone routing conflict requires re-routing water service away from frontage | `moderate` |
   124→| Site within 100 ft of moonlight tower or guy wire — permit required, no prohibition | `moderate` |
   125→| Light rail corridor proximity (non-4th Street) — UROP consultation required | `moderate` |
   126→| Service-load size pushes project from Service-Only to Design Services ESPA path | `note` |
   127→| Standard AE plan notes verbatim compliance | `note` |
   128→| Addressing plan / street-name reservation required for new private drives | `note` |
   129→| Existing AE facility locations not field-verified (only AE record-drawing data) | `data-gap` |
   130→| Moonlight tower proximity unknown (downtown / central Austin site without field survey) | `data-gap` |
   131→| AE Service Availability uncertain at parcel (edge of service territory) | `data-gap` |
   132→
   133→## Common pitfalls
   134→
   135→- Treating "the utility provider operates overhead in the vicinity" as authorization to leave the building-to-property-line service overhead on a CTC, Urban Roadway, Plaza Saltillo TOD, NBG, or Hill Country frontage — undergrounding is mandatory regardless.
   136→- Anchoring overhead clearance dimensions to the **pole centerline** rather than the **outermost conductor** — on three-phase configurations the outer conductor may be several feet offset; clearances that appear adequate on plan can be non-compliant in the field.
   137→- Conflating the UCM § 1.10.3 universal 7.5-ft / 15-ft clearances (apply everywhere overhead AE exists) with the LDC Subchapter E 10-ft overhead utility zone (applies only on CTC / Urban Roadway / Plaza Saltillo / NBG). Both can apply simultaneously on those frontages; only UCM 1.10.3 applies elsewhere.
   138→- Assuming AULCC is universal — it is only triggered by the four specific thresholds. Small infill projects often slide under and shouldn't carry AULCC time in the schedule.
   139→- Citing **§ 14-11-205** for the 100-ft moonlight tower permit — that section is the 25-ft ROW prohibition. The 100-ft permit threshold is **§ 14-11-201**.
   140→- Citing **LDC § 25-9-173** for service availability — this section does not exist; correct authority is AEDC §§ 1.4.1 / 1.3.2.
   141→- Accepting an Address Validation Letter (AVL) as an approved addressing plan — they are distinct; the addressing plan must be separately approved by AMS before site plan approval.
   142→- Assuming Hill Country undergrounding applies near US 183 or US 290 West — LDC § 25-2-1104(A) carves these out; only the five named Hill Country Roadways trigger § 25-2-1125.
   143→- Drawing transformer pad in the public ROW or labeling its area as parkland — both prohibited; the pad must be on customer property within a dedicated AE easement.
   144→- Treating UCM § 2.9.1.A.1 as the basis for pole/transmission separation rules — that section governs easement width, not pole placement; the pole-placement requirement currently lacks a confirmed code anchor and should be coordinated with AE directly.
   145→- Routing non-electrical utilities parallel within an AE / public utility easement boundary — only perpendicular (up to 45°) crossings are permitted.
   146→- Failing to budget post-approval ESPA time — ESPA is submitted after site plan approval; AE design can run 6–12 weeks (Service-Only) to 16+ weeks (Design Services / Network Area) before an Electric Permit number is issued, gating downstream work.
   147→- Confusing the Building Service Planning Application (BSPA — required for building permits with exterior modifications) with the ESPA (required for new/modified electric service). Both can apply.
   148→- Sizing transformer pads to a "standard" 10×10 dimension — pad dimensions are determined by AE Design based on the customer's AutoCAD submittal (UCM § 1.5.2.6); no universal fixed dimension exists in code text.
   149→- Showing a vault near overhead power lines with a plan note "vault approved by AE Design" but no AE written clearance letter in the project file — UCM § 1.10.3 requires the letter to be filed, not merely referenced.
   150→- Routing AE underground conduit in a joint trench with other utilities without a written AE joint-trench agreement (UCM § 1.10.5.A) — the 12-in separation rule covers perpendicular crossings only; parallel/joint runs require the separate agreement.

# Environmental Findings — 12713 Cinchring Ln

**Property:** 12713 Cinchring Ln, Austin, TX 78727 — Lot 12, Block M, Scofield Subdivision
**Proposed use:** Demolish existing SFR (built 1993); build ground-up duplex (2 units)
**Lot:** ~7,840 sq ft (0.18 acres), SF-2 zoning
**Watershed:** Walnut Creek — Suburban classification
**Date:** 2026-06-03

---

## Summary

- **No high-severity environmental barriers** to the proposed duplex. The site is outside the Edwards Aquifer recharge/contributing zone (no EAPP), outside the 100-year and 500-year floodplain (Zone X), and carries no known Critical Environmental Features.
- **Asbestos survey is required before demolition** of the 1993 house under TCEQ NESHAP regulations (40 CFR 61, Subpart M); lead-based paint screening is also recommended given the pre-1996 construction date.
- **No Phase I ESA has been performed** — a recognized data gap. Residential use history suggests low contamination risk, but a Phase I is recommended before demolition to document the absence of Recognized Environmental Conditions and satisfy lender/investor due diligence.
- **BCCP participation fee applies** at building permit issuance; no individual USFWS Section 7 or Section 10 consultation is anticipated.
- **Tree protection, floodplain, and stormwater** matters are cross-referenced to their respective disciplines (eptp, fwp, sde) and are not duplicated here.

---

## Findings

### 1. Walnut Creek Suburban Watershed Classification

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** Austin LDC Ch. 25-8, Sec. 25-8-2; Ch. 25-8 Article 9 (Suburban Watershed Requirements)
**Finding:** The property lies within the Walnut Creek watershed, classified as Suburban under Chapter 25-8. Suburban watershed rules (Article 9) govern impervious cover limits and water quality controls. For this lot, the SF-2 zoning IC limit of 45% is expected to control over the watershed IC limit, but the more restrictive of the two applies. Water quality controls (sedimentation/filtration per ECM Sec. 1.6.0) are required for redevelopment; however, the Scofield subdivision may already be served by regional water quality facilities, which could satisfy the lot-level obligation.
**Implication for the developer:** The suburban watershed classification does not block the project but establishes the regulatory framework for impervious cover and water quality. Confirm whether existing regional controls serve this lot — if not, an on-site SCM may be required.
**Recommended next step:** Confirm lot-level IC limit and regional WQ facility coverage with the Watershed Protection Department during pre-application. Cross-reference stormwater controls to the **sde** discipline.

---

### 2. Not in Edwards Aquifer Recharge or Contributing Zone

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** TCEQ 30 TAC Chapter 213; Travis County Aquifer Maps
**Finding:** The property is not within the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone (EARZ) or Contributing Zone. The EARZ in Travis County is concentrated south of the Colorado River over exposed Edwards Group limestones. North Austin (Scofield area) overlies different geologic formations. No TCEQ Edwards Aquifer Protection Plan (EAPP) is required.
**Implication for the developer:** Eliminates the EAPP application, associated engineering, and TCEQ review timeline from the project scope. This is favorable.
**Recommended next step:** None required.

---

### 3. No Known Critical Environmental Features

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** Austin LDC Sec. 25-8-281 et seq.; ECM Sec. 1.10.0; City of Austin Watershed Protection karst database
**Finding:** CEFs in Austin include springs, caves, sinkholes, point recharge features, rimrock, and bluffs. No known CEFs have been identified at or immediately adjacent to 12713 Cinchring Ln. The site's geology (Cretaceous formations in north Austin, not Edwards Limestone) carries low probability of karst features. The City's karst database (~550 points) is concentrated in western and southwestern Austin.
**Implication for the developer:** Low risk. However, an Environmental Resource Inventory (ERI) form is required as part of the building permit application, and Watershed Protection staff will make the formal CEF determination during review. If a CEF were identified, a 150-ft to 300-ft protective buffer would encumber the lot — on a 7,840 sq ft parcel, this would be project-fatal.
**Recommended next step:** Complete the ERI form at permitting. No pre-application CEF investigation is warranted given the low geological probability.

---

### 4. BCCP Participation Area — Fee Applies

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** USFWS Balcones Canyonlands Conservation Plan (BCCP), 1996; Travis County BCCP participation area maps
**Finding:** The property is within the BCCP participation area. The BCCP provides an Incidental Take Permit covering development within the permit area for 14 federally listed species (including golden-cheeked warbler and six karst invertebrates). The site — a fully developed suburban lot — does not contain warbler nesting habitat or known karst invertebrate habitat. The BCCP Participation Fee is collected at building permit issuance.
**Implication for the developer:** The fee is a modest line item (typically a few hundred dollars for residential development). No individual USFWS consultation is needed.
**Recommended next step:** Budget for the BCCP fee. Confirm current fee schedule with DSD at time of permit application.

---

### 5. No Wetlands Expected

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** USFWS National Wetlands Inventory (NWI); Clean Water Act Section 404
**Finding:** The site is an upland suburban lot in Zone X (no floodplain), on well-drained soils with no surface water features on or adjacent to the parcel. No jurisdictional wetlands are expected. No Section 404 permit or Army Corps of Engineers coordination is anticipated.
**Implication for the developer:** No wetland constraints on site layout or construction sequencing.
**Recommended next step:** Confirm via NWI Wetlands Mapper for documentation completeness. A formal wetland delineation is not warranted.

---

### 6. Phase I ESA Not Performed

**Severity:** data-gap
**Citation:** ASTM E1527-21 (Standard Practice for Environmental Site Assessments)
**Finding:** No Phase I ESA has been commissioned for the property. The site has been in single-family residential use since the subdivision was developed in the early 1990s; prior use was rangeland/agricultural. No TCEQ State Superfund, EPA NPL, or LUST sites have been identified at this address in available databases. The contamination risk profile is low. However, without a Phase I, potential concerns — historical agricultural chemicals, adjacent-parcel USTs, vapor intrusion — cannot be formally excluded.
**Implication for the developer:** Most lenders and investors require a Phase I ESA for acquisition or construction financing. The absence of a Phase I does not block permitting but creates a due-diligence gap. The low-risk residential history makes an adverse finding unlikely, but the assessment is the documentation vehicle.
**Recommended next step:** Commission a Phase I ESA (ASTM E1527-21) before demolition. This can run concurrent with design; typical turnaround is 3-4 weeks, cost $2,000-$4,000.

---

### 7. Asbestos Survey Required Before Demolition (TCEQ NESHAP)

**Severity:** moderate
**Citation:** 40 CFR 61, Subpart M (National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants — Asbestos); TCEQ Asbestos Program; Texas DSHS Asbestos Health Protection Rules (25 TAC 295)
**Finding:** The existing house was built in 1993. Asbestos-containing materials (ACM) were used in residential construction through the mid-1990s, particularly in floor tiles, joint compound, roofing materials, pipe insulation, and textite siding. Under the federal NESHAP rule, the owner/operator must conduct a thorough asbestos inspection of a facility before demolition, performed by a Texas-licensed asbestos inspector. If ACM is found, abatement must be completed by a licensed contractor before demolition, and a 10-working-day notification to TCEQ is required prior to the start of demolition or abatement.
**Implication for the developer:** This is a hard prerequisite to demolition. The inspection adds 1-2 weeks; if ACM is found, abatement adds 2-4 weeks and $3,000-$15,000+ depending on materials and quantities. Schedule the inspection early.
**Recommended next step:** Engage a Texas-licensed asbestos inspector to survey the existing structure. If ACM is identified, obtain abatement bids and factor cost/schedule into the demolition plan. File the TCEQ 10-day notification before any demolition activity.

---

### 8. Lead-Based Paint Screening Recommended

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** 40 CFR 745 (Lead-Based Paint); HUD/EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) Rule; Texas DSHS 25 TAC 295 Subchapter I
**Finding:** The house was built in 1993. The Consumer Product Safety Commission banned lead-based paint for residential use in 1978, so the structure is unlikely to contain LBP. However, lead can be present in plumbing solder (pre-1986 ban) and in some specialty coatings. For a full demolition, lead risk is minimal but should be addressed as part of the asbestos/hazmat survey scope.
**Implication for the developer:** Low likelihood of encountering LBP. Including lead screening in the asbestos survey scope adds negligible marginal cost.
**Recommended next step:** Include LBP screening in the asbestos inspection scope as a precautionary measure.

---

### 9. Low Contamination Risk — Residential History

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** TCEQ State Superfund and LUST databases; EPA NPL
**Finding:** The Scofield subdivision was platted and built as a residential community in the late 1980s through 1990s. Prior land use was undeveloped rangeland. No TCEQ Superfund, LUST, or EPA NPL sites have been identified at this address. Surrounding land uses are residential and low-density commercial. The contamination risk is low and consistent with typical suburban residential property.
**Implication for the developer:** No brownfield or remediation concerns are anticipated. A Phase I ESA (Finding 6) would provide formal documentation.
**Recommended next step:** Addressed via Phase I ESA recommendation (Finding 6).

---

### 10. Floodplain — Zone X, No Constraints

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** FEMA FIRM Panel 48453C0115E, effective 06/16/1993; property survey
**Finding:** The property is in FEMA Zone X, outside both the 100-year and 500-year floodplain. No floodplain development permit, CLOMR/LOMR, or elevation certificate is required. The site sits at approximately 850-870 ft elevation, well above the Walnut Creek floodplain corridor.
**Implication for the developer:** No floodplain constraints on building design, finished floor elevation, or construction sequencing.
**Recommended next step:** None. Cross-reference to the **fwp** discipline for any local drainage or creek-buffer considerations.

---

### 11. Tree Protection — Cross-Reference to eptp

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** Austin LDC Ch. 25-8, Subchapter B (Tree and Natural Area Protection)
**Finding:** Austin's tree protection ordinance applies to all development. Heritage trees (19+ inches diameter at 4.5 ft) require a removal permit with mitigation; protected trees (8+ inches) require mitigation if removed. The lot may contain mature trees established during or after subdivision development (30+ years of growth). A tree survey is required as part of the building permit application.
**Implication for the developer:** Heritage or protected trees, if present, could constrain the building footprint or require mitigation fees. On a 7,840 sq ft lot with 40% max building coverage, tree locations materially affect site layout.
**Recommended next step:** This is fully addressed in the **eptp** discipline. Conduct a tree survey early in design to inform footprint placement.

---

### 12. Soil Conditions — High Shrink-Swell Clay

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** USDA Web Soil Survey; Blackland Prairie ecological region data
**Finding:** The site is in the Blackland Prairie region with deep, dark, clay-rich Vertisol soils (likely Houston Black clay series). These soils have high shrink-swell potential, expanding when wet and contracting when dry. This is the dominant foundation risk in the Austin area.
**Implication for the developer:** An engineered foundation (post-tensioned slab or drilled piers) is required. A geotechnical report should inform foundation design.
**Recommended next step:** Commission a geotechnical investigation before foundation design. Typical cost $2,500-$5,000; turnaround 2-3 weeks.

---

### 13. Wildfire Risk — Low

**Severity:** note
**Citation:** City of Austin Wildfire Division; Texas Wildfire Risk Assessment Portal (TxWRAP)
**Finding:** Scofield Farms is a flat, fully developed suburban neighborhood with no wildland-urban interface exposure. Wildfire risk in Austin is concentrated in the Edwards Plateau / Hill Country areas to the west and southwest. This site is classified as low wildfire risk.
**Implication for the developer:** No wildfire-specific construction standards are triggered.
**Recommended next step:** None. Confirm WUI boundary status via Austin GIS if HOME Phase 2 fire-resistive construction standards become relevant to a future subdivision scenario.

---

## Open Questions for the Engineer

1. **Regional water quality controls:** Does the Scofield subdivision have existing regional WQ facilities that serve Lot 12, Block M? If so, the lot-level on-site SCM requirement may be satisfied. Confirm with Watershed Protection Department.

2. **Asbestos survey results:** Until the asbestos inspection is complete, the demolition schedule and cost carry uncertainty. Are there any known renovation or abatement records for the existing house?

3. **Geotechnical conditions:** Has any prior geotechnical work been performed on adjacent lots in this section of Scofield that could inform foundation assumptions before commissioning a site-specific investigation?

4. **Phase I ESA scope:** Will the developer's lender require a Phase I ESA? If so, this should be initiated immediately to avoid holding up the closing or construction loan timeline.

5. **Existing sanitary sewer vault:** The seed data notes a concrete sanitary sewer vault on site. What is the vault's function and disposition plan — remove, cap, or re-use? Austin Water should confirm before demolition planning is finalized. (Cross-reference to **wwp** discipline.)
